q: A 45-year-old man presents with inability to abduct the shoulder after a fall onto the left shoulder. Examination shows flattening of the deltoid contour and diminished sensation over the lateral aspect of the shoulder ("regimental badge" area). Which nerve is most likely injured?
ex: The axillary nerve (C5, C6) winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and supplies the deltoid and teres minor. It is commonly injured in shoulder dislocation or surgical neck fracture, causing deltoid paralysis (flattened shoulder, weak abduction) and sensory loss over the regimental badge area. Suprascapular nerve injury weakens abduction but spares sensation; long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula; radial nerve injury spares the deltoid.

q: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia. Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected. Which of the following enzymes, dependent on thiamine as a cofactor, is most commonly used as a diagnostic test for this deficiency?
ex: Thiamine (B1) is the cofactor for transketolase (HMP shunt), pyruvate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Reduced erythrocyte transketolase activity (with increased stimulation by added TPP, the "TPP effect") is the standard laboratory test for thiamine deficiency, as in Wernicke encephalopathy.

q: A 35-year-old woman with chronic iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 8 g/dL) complains of easy fatigability on exertion. Which of the following physiological adaptations is BEST expected in her?
o: Decreased erythrocyte 2,3-BPG causing a left shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve
Increased erythrocyte 2,3-BPG causing a right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve
Increased hemoglobin affinity for oxygen to enhance loading in the lungs
Reduced cardiac output to decrease tissue oxygen consumption
ex: Chronic hypoxia (anemia) increases erythrocyte 2,3-BPG, which binds deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the T state, shifting the O2-Hb dissociation curve to the right. This lowers Hb affinity for O2, enhancing O2 unloading to tissues and compensating for reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. A left shift (as in CO poisoning, alkalosis, hypothermia, stored blood) would impair tissue oxygenation.

q: A 35-year-old man presents with jaundice, fatigue, and right upper quadrant discomfort. Serology is positive for anti-HBs and anti-HBc (IgG), but negative for HBsAg. Liver biopsy shows piecemeal necrosis and a "piecemeal" lymphocytic infiltrate eroding the limiting plate. Which statement about this patient's liver disease is most accurate?
o: He has chronic active hepatitis B with ongoing viral replication, as indicated by HBsAg negativity
He has chronic hepatitis B in the replicative phase; HBsAg negativity is a false-negative result
He has chronic hepatitis C co-infection; hepatitis B serology is merely past exposure
He has chronic active hepatitis with active viral replication, likely hepatitis C, given HBsAg negativity and anti-HBc IgG positivity
ex: Chronic active hepatitis (CAH) shows piecemeal necrosis—lymphocytic infiltration destroying hepatocytes at the limiting plate. HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive (IgG) with anti-HBs indicates past hepatitis B exposure, but active piecemeal necrosis in a serology profile that excludes HBV replication points to chronic hepatitis C as the more likely etiology.

q: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and heart failure (LVEF 35%) is started on a drug to improve glycemic control. Two weeks later, he develops severe diarrhea, nausea, and dizziness, and his renal function is found to be deteriorating. Which drug was most likely started?
ex: Empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor) is preferred in T2DM with heart failure; however, it can cause volume depletion (diarrhea, nausea, dizziness) and acute kidney injury, especially in patients on diuretics or with poor renal perfusion. Metformin causes lactic acidosis with renal impairment but not this pattern; pioglitazone worsens heart failure (fluid retention); sitagliptin is generally weight-neutral.

q: A 24-year-old woman presents with abrupt fever, severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. CSF analysis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly raised protein, and normal glucose. She improved clinically but later developed behavioral changes and memory loss. Which organism is the most likely cause?
ex: HSV-1 causes sporadic encephalitis with predilection for temporal lobes; CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose, and patients often develop personality changes and memory loss. Bacterial meningitis (Neisseria, Streptococcus) shows neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose; TB meningitis has low CSF glucose with lymphocytic predominance.

q: A 45-year-old man is found dead in a lake after 2 days. Autopsy shows frothy fluid in the trachea and bronchi, emphysema aquosum, and edematous lungs. Which of the following findings is the most conclusive evidence that death was due to drowning?
o: Presence of froth in the airways and nostrils
Presence of diatoms in the bone marrow of the femur
Wrinkled, sodden 'washerwoman' skin of the palms and soles
ex: Diatoms in bone marrow or other closed organs prove ante-mortem aspiration of water during drowning, as they reach deep tissues only via the circulation. Froth, emphysema aquosum, and washerwoman skin can occur in bodies immersed in water after death and are not diagnostic of drowning.

q: A village of 2000 people is surveyed in January 2026. At the start of the month, 20 residents already had chickenpox; during the month, 40 new cases developed. What is the incidence rate of chickenpox for January?
ex: Incidence = new cases / population at risk during the period. Those already infected (20) are not at risk, so population at risk = 2000 − 20 = 1980; 40/1980 × 100 = 2.02%. Option C (60/2000) is prevalence, which counts all existing cases.

q: A 35-year-old woman presents with slowly progressive hearing loss in both ears, worse on the right, with tinnitus. Otoscopy shows intact, normal-looking tympanic membranes bilaterally. Pure tone audiometry reveals bilateral conductive hearing loss with a Carhart notch on the right. Stapedial reflex is absent on the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Bilateral conductive deafness with an intact tympanic membrane, Carhart notch on audiometry, and absent stapedial reflex indicate stapes footplate fixation—classic otosclerosis. Menière disease causes fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss with vertigo; acoustic neuroma causes unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus; CSOM is associated with tympanic membrane perforation and discharge.

q: A 65-year-old woman presents with sudden onset severe pain and redness in the right eye, headache, nausea and blurred vision. Examination reveals a mid-dilated, non-reactive pupil, hazy cornea, and intraocular pressure of 48 mmHg. The most likely diagnosis is:
ex: Acute primary angle-closure glaucoma causes sudden rise in IOP due to iris blocking the aqueous outflow (trabecular meshwork), classically in elderly hypermetropic women. It presents with painful red eye, headache, nausea/vomiting, corneal edema (hazy cornea), mid-dilated fixed pupil, and markedly elevated IOP. It is an ophthalmic emergency — treatment aims at rapid IOP reduction (acetazolamide, hyperosmotics, pilocarpine, beta-blockers) followed by laser iridotomy to prevent irreversible optic nerve damage.

q: A 45-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites presents with fever and abdominal pain of 2 days' duration. Ascitic fluid analysis shows a polymorphonuclear (PMN) count of 400/mm3. What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic therapy?
ex: Ascitic fluid PMN count >=250/mm3 confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), a complication of cirrhosis with ascites. Empiric therapy is an intravenous third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime), which covers the most common pathogens (E. coli, Klebsiella). Oral quinolones are used for SBP prophylaxis, not treatment; aminoglycosides are avoided due to nephrotoxicity.

q: A 55-year-old man presents with colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, progressive abdominal distension, and absolute constipation of 24 hours duration. He underwent appendicectomy 10 years ago. Erect abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels with a "step-ladder" pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Step-ladder air-fluid levels on X-ray, colicky pain, and absolute constipation localize to the small bowel; prior abdominal surgery makes adhesive obstruction the most common cause. Paralytic ileus is painless with absent bowel sounds and diffuse dilation without step-ladder levels; large bowel obstruction shows peripheral/distal dilated loops; mesenteric ischemia presents with pain out of proportion to signs.

q: A 28-year-old woman, G3P2L2 at 34 weeks of gestation, presents with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain and moderate vaginal bleeding for 2 hours. She has pregnancy-induced hypertension. On examination, the uterus is tense and tender (woody feel), fetal parts are not palpable, and fetal heart sounds are absent. Per speculum, dark red blood is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Abruptio placentae (premature separation of normally implanted placenta) classically presents with painful, dark vaginal bleeding, a tense "woody" uterus, and fetal distress or death; PIH is a major risk factor. Placenta previa causes PAINLESS bright red bleeding. Uterine rupture typically follows a scarred uterus with maternal collapse. Vasa previa bleeds at membrane rupture, with fetal blood loss and sudden fetal distress.

q: An 8-month-old infant presents with 2 days of low-grade fever, barking cough, and hoarse voice. On examination: inspiratory stridor at rest with suprasternal retractions, SpO2 96% on room air, chest is clear. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
ex: Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup), usually due to parainfluenza virus, causes subglottic oedema manifesting as barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor. Stridor at rest indicates moderate-severe obstruction; nebulised adrenaline gives rapid relief (within 30 min) and dexamethasone reduces airway oedema. Antibiotics are not indicated (viral aetiology), and salbutamol is for lower airway bronchospasm.

q: A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia, started on haloperidol 20 mg/day one week ago, presents with high-grade fever (104°F), severe generalized muscle rigidity, diaphoresis, fluctuating consciousness, and labile blood pressure. Investigations: serum CPK 12,000 IU/L and leukocytosis (14,000/mm³). What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: NMS is an idiosyncratic, potentially fatal reaction to antipsychotics (especially high-potency typicals like haloperidol), typically appearing days to weeks after starting or dose escalation. Classic tetrad: hyperthermia, severe muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered consciousness, with markedly elevated CPK. Serotonin syndrome (SSRI/MAOI use) features hyperreflexia and clonus rather than lead-pipe rigidity; malignant hyperthermia follows inhalational anesthetics/succinylcholine in susceptible patients; tardive dyskinesia is a late, chronic movement disorder without fever. Management: stop the antipsychotic and provide supportive care; dantrolene and bromocriptine may be used.

q: A 32-year-old man undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anaesthesia develops masseter muscle spasm followed by generalized muscle rigidity, rapidly rising end-tidal CO2 (65 mmHg), tachycardia, and a temperature rise to 39.5°C. Arterial blood gas shows metabolic and respiratory acidosis. Which drug combination most likely triggered this condition?
ex: Malignant hyperthermia is a hypermetabolic syndrome triggered by succinylcholine and volatile inhalational anaesthetics (e.g., sevoflurane, halothane) in genetically susceptible patients (RYR1 mutation). Stop triggers, give IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg, hyperventilate with 100% O2, cool and correct acidosis. Propofol, opioids, benzodiazepines and non-depolarizing relaxants are safe in MH-susceptible patients.

q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with bilious vomiting. Supine abdominal radiograph shows a "double bubble" sign with no distal bowel gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Double bubble sign (air in stomach and proximal duodenum, absent distal gas) is the classic finding of duodenal atresia, the commonest cause of neonatal duodenal obstruction; strongly associated with Down syndrome. Malrotation with volvulus can also cause a double bubble but usually shows some distal bowel gas or other features; meconium ileus and Hirschsprung disease cause distal obstruction without this sign.

q: A 25-year-old man falls on his outstretched right hand. He has wrist pain with tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox; plain radiographs are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure the patient and allow full activity
Reduce a suspected Colles fracture and apply a below-elbow cast
Immobilize in a thumb spica cast and repeat radiographs in 2 weeks
Immediately proceed to MRI of the wrist
ex: Snuffbox tenderness after FOOSH indicates scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise; up to 20% are radiographically occult initially. Treat as fracture: thumb spica cast and repeat X-ray in 10-14 days (MRI if still symptomatic). Retrograde blood supply makes proximal pole at risk of AVN/nonunion if untreated.

q: A 28-year-old man presents with intensely pruritic lesions over finger webs, wrists, and scrotum for 4 weeks. Itching worsens at night. Examination shows erythematous papules and thin, greyish, wavy burrow-like tracks on the finger webs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Burrow-like tracks in finger webs with nocturnal pruritus and genital involvement are classic for scabies, caused by Sarcoptes scabiei. Diagnosis confirmed by identifying the mite, eggs, or scybala on skin scrapings; treat with topical permethrin 5% applied to the whole body (including fingernail folds), repeated after 1 week, with treatment of close contacts.

q: A 45-year-old man sustains a fracture of the midshaft of the humerus. He presents with wrist drop and inability to extend the metacarpophalangeal joints. Which nerve is most likely injured?
ex: The radial nerve winds around the humerus in the radial (spiral) groove and is the most commonly injured nerve in midshaft humeral fractures. Injury causes wrist drop (loss of wrist and MCP joint extension) with sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand, including the anatomical snuffbox.

q: An 8-year-old boy develops acute hemolytic anemia with dark urine 2 days after eating fava beans. Peripheral smear shows Heinz bodies and bite cells. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible?
ex: G6PD is the first enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway, generating NADPH needed to regenerate reduced glutathione, which protects RBCs from oxidative damage. Favism (fava bean ingestion) triggers oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies in G6PD deficiency. Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia without Heinz bodies; hexokinase and glucose-6-phosphatase deficiencies are not associated with favism-induced hemolysis.

q: A 58-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 15 mL/min/1.73 m²) presents with fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Investigations: Hb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 88 fL (normocytic, normochromic), reticulocyte count 0.5% (low). Which of the following is the most likely cause of this anemia?
ex: Chronic kidney disease causes normocytic normochromic anemia with inappropriately low reticulocyte count due to decreased erythropoietin (EPO) secretion by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts of the kidney. B12/folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia; iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia — all usually show an elevated reticulocyte count (unless combined with EPO loss).

q: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive breathlessness and dry cough. Chest X-ray shows bilateral reticulonodular opacities. Lung biopsy shows destruction of alveolar walls with cyst formation and "honeycombing" on microscopy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Honeycomb lung with patchy interstitial fibrosis and fibroblastic foci is characteristic of UIP (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis). Sarcoidosis shows non-caseating granulomas; bronchopneumonia shows patchy suppurative inflammation; alveolar proteinosis shows PAS-positive eosinophilic granular material filling alveoli.

q: A 55-year-old hypertensive man on amlodipine and metoprolol presents with painful swelling and redness of the great toe, with serum uric acid 9.2 mg/dL and normal renal function. Which drug should be AVOIDED if a diuretic is added for uncontrolled hypertension?
ex: Thiazide diuretics (HCTZ) reduce uric acid excretion by competing for the organic anion transporter in the proximal tubule, raising serum urate and precipitating gout. Losartan is uricosuric; spironolactone and amiloride have no significant hyperuricemic effect.

q: A 28-year-old man presents with profuse watery diarrhea of 6 hours' duration. His stools are described as "rice water". He is severely dehydrated with sunken eyes and poor skin turgor. Which is the most likely causative organism?
ex: "Rice-water" stool with rapid, severe dehydration is classic of cholera. V. cholerae produces cholera toxin, which binds GM1 ganglioside and activates adenylate cyclase, causing massive isotonic fluid secretion. Management is aggressive fluid/electrolyte replacement plus doxycycline. Shigella causes bloody mucoid dysentery, S. Typhi causes enteric fever, and ETEC causes travelers' diarrhea with milder dehydration.

q: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department unconscious, with alcohol on his breath. On examination, his pupils are unequal and sluggishly reactive to light. What is the most appropriate next step?
ex: Unequal pupils (anisocoria) are not explained by alcoholic intoxication alone; they suggest an intracranial lesion such as traumatic subdural/epidural hematoma. Alcoholic coma must never be presumed until head injury is excluded — CT head is mandatory.

q: A 6-member family has one child with measles. Within one incubation period, 3 of the 5 susceptible siblings develop measles. Which epidemiological measure does this represent?
ex: Secondary attack rate = (number of exposed susceptible contacts developing disease within one incubation period ÷ total exposed susceptible contacts) × 100. Here, 3/5 = 60%. It measures the infectivity/transmissibility of an agent and spread within a household.

q: A 62-year-old diabetic man presents with severe right otalgia and purulent otorrhea for 3 weeks, unresponsive to topical antibiotic ear drops. Examination reveals granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the right external auditory canal. Which is the most likely causative organism?
ex: Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa occurs in elderly diabetics/immunocompromised patients. Pseudomonas aeruginosa invades the skull base through the external auditory canal; granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction is characteristic. The facial nerve is the earliest cranial nerve affected.

q: A 60-year-old diabetic man presents with sudden, painless loss of vision in the right eye. Fundus examination shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Sudden painless vision loss with pale retina and cherry-red spot is classic central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The cherry-red spot is the intact foveal choroid visible through the thin fovea against the surrounding ischemic, edematous retina. CRVO causes diffuse retinal hemorrhages ("blood and thunder"), retinal detachment causes a gray elevated retina with a tear, and vitreous hemorrhage causes loss of the red reflex.

q: A 50-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis presents with gradually increasing abdominal distension. Ascitic fluid analysis shows: total protein 1.5 g/dL, albumin 0.8 g/dL. Serum albumin is 3.2 g/dL. Based on the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG), what is the most likely cause of ascites?
ex: SAAG = serum albumin − ascitic fluid albumin = 3.2 − 0.8 = 2.4 g/dL. A SAAG of ≥1.1 g/dL indicates ascites due to portal hypertension (cirrhosis, cardiac ascites, hepatic venous outflow obstruction); SAAG <1.1 g/dL suggests non-portal causes such as malignancy, tuberculous peritonitis, or nephrotic syndrome.

q: A 60-year-old man presents with jaundice, pruritus, and painless progressive obstructive jaundice over 6 weeks. Ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts with a normal-caliber common bile duct and a distended, palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
ex: Painless progressive obstructive jaundice with a palpable, distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) in an elderly patient is classic for periampullary carcinoma, most commonly carcinoma of the head of the pancreas. Choledocholithiasis usually causes painful, fluctuating jaundice with a non-palpable gallbladder. Gallbladder carcinoma presents with right upper quadrant pain and a lump, while acute cholangitis features Charcot triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain).
